title: Multi-expert Prompting Improves Reliability, Safety and Usefulness of Large Language Models

reviews.summary: This paper proposes "Multi-expert prompting," extending the idea of ExpertPrompting (Xu et al., 2023) by expanding it to multiple experts (original ExpertPrompting conditions the model on a single expert). It differs from the original work first by conditioning multiple experts, hence potentially getting more diverse generations, then applying a group decision-making method (Nominal group technique, NGT), which uses a 7-step process to produce a group response. At an implementation level, multiple expert responses are generated with an expert-conditioning prompt - these responses are aggregated into an aggregation prompt, which results in a final conclusion from the multiple responses.
reviews.strengths:
1. The proposed method is pragmatic and easy to implement, and the experiment results demonstrate the method's efficacy.
2. The paper is easy to follow and explains the method well.
3. Applying a method from social science to NLP is an interesting twist - I couldn't have thought of this.

Note: My previous review raised concerns on point 2, which have since been addressed in the current revision.
reviews.weaknesses:
Section 5.2 conducts an ablation study on which steps of the NGT method have different effects, followed by an expert count vs performance experiment. I have a suspicion that the characteristics of this would be different based on the model size - but the authors only discuss GPT. The latter (number of experts), in particular, would likely vary depending on whether the pre-train corpus has diverse (in particular, not open) data used for training.

The method has no countermeasures against hallucinating experts. For example, if the model has been poorly trained on a specific domain (e.g., poor/biased training data for said domain), a hallucinating expert on that topic can have adversarial effects on the response quality. An extreme version of that would be a (majority) mixture of hallucinating experts (e.g., the minority is factual, but gets drowned out in consensus). The authors discuss weighting in the limitations, which can be a potential mitigation - but I would like to see a bit more discussion from the authors on this matter as a limitation of their work.
